problem: The stated condition for the stability guarantee is incomplete. With Q ≥ 0 only (the chapter itself allows zero diagonal entries in Q) and (A, B) controllable, the Riccati equation can have a positive semidefinite solution whose closed loop A − BK still has an unstable pole. Example: A = diag(1, −1), B = [1; 1], Q = diag(0, 1), R = 1 is controllable, P = diag(0, 0.414) solves the ARE, yet A − BK has a pole at +1 because the unstable state carries zero weight in Q.
fix: Add the standard extra condition: the guarantee holds when (A, B) is stabilisable and (Q^(1/2), A) is detectable — simpler sufficient version: (A, B) controllable and Q > 0 (strictly positive definite), R > 0. Then A − BK has all eigenvalues in the open left half plane. State the same full condition in the Quiz Q3 answer.

where: Section 3, sentence 'R must be strictly positive, never zero, because free control makes the cost unbounded'
problem: The cost cannot become unbounded: the integrand xᵀQx + uᵀRu is non-negative. What fails with R = 0 is the problem itself — it becomes singular and the optimal input may be unbounded (impulsive), so no finite gain exists.
fix: Write: 'R must be strictly positive definite, never zero. With R = 0 the problem is singular: control is free, the optimal input can grow without bound (impulsive), and no finite LQR gain exists.'

problem: The answer explains the choice of the positive semidefinite solution only through 'feedback sign'. The sign of K is decided by P itself; the real reason is that P defines the optimal cost-to-go J* = xᵀPx, which is a squared quantity and so cannot be negative. The other roots are not valid value functions and give a saddle or unstable closed loop.
fix: Answer: 'P is the cost-to-go matrix, so the optimal cost from state x is xᵀPx ≥ 0; only the positive semidefinite solution is a valid value function. Any other root gives a closed loop that is not stable (in the scalar example the negative root gives K = −2.414 and pole +1.414).'
